Albanese says AI must be subject of public discussion now
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the artificial intelligence must now be to subject of public discussion.
The prime minister says while is has the potential to improve people's lives and productivity, it carries risks.
He's also spoken about the recent OpenAI data hack that affected a Services Australia portal.

"Recently an Artificial Intelligence agent infiltrated an Australian government website. This is unacceptable. And it is why Australia has been leading the way in establishing Australian Standards for AI," Albanese says."Standards to ensure AI will work and deliver for people — not the other way around. We can't ignore AI or prevent it."

"Standards to ensure AI will work and deliver for people — not the other way around. We can't ignore AI or prevent it."
World must 'embrace change and reform', Albanese says
Anthony Albanese says the world must "embrace change and reform" if it wants to create a world of human dignity.
He says Australia doesn't believe in abandonning multilateralism, but rather reforming it to adapt to challenges ahead.
The PM says Australia seeks to amplify the voices of mid-sized states to ensure Security Council decisions are informed by a wide range of perspectives.
He says Australia stands for a "safer world" where "no country dominates, and no country is dominated".
"In our region, the Indo-Pacific, we are elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice, free from coercion," Albanese says.

"So that our partners can address the big issues confronting them: economic security, human development, energy security, transnational crime, sovereign capabilities, trade and investment, and science and technology."
PM makes his pitch for Australia's seat on UN Security Council
The prime minister is now making his pitch for Australia's non-permanent seat at the UN Security Council from 2029 to 2030.
Anthony Albanese says Australia wants to respond to the world's challenges by partnering to make a difference.
He says should Australia's bid be successful, Australia will listen with respect, partner as equal and protect what matters most.

"As a member of the UN Security Council, Australia will safeguard the rules that protect us all by upholding international law, including the UN Charter, and the sovereignty of all states," Albanese says.

"We will amplify the voices of small states and middle powers to ensure a wider range of perspectives shape the Council's decisions."We will work to prevent crises, resolve conflicts and protect civilians through diplomacy, peacebuilding and practical action."

Albanese says UN mission can't be entrusted alone by great powers
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says from artificial intelligence to climate change, the world is being confronted by challenges predecessors could never have imagined.
He says the world can rise to meet new challenges now to reaffirm national sovereignty and shared humanity.
Albanese says smaller countries need to take more responsibility for the world's challenges.
"We understand the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers, or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone," Albanese says.
"Nor can it be sub-contracted to the world's richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology."Then, now, and always, shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us."

Albanese begins speech to UN General Assembly
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just taken to the podium at the United Nations General Assembly in New York to speak.
He's started by saying that eight decades ago, the citizens and leaders of nations around the world made "solemn promise" to never repeat the horrors of World War II and nuclear weapons.
Albanese has urged world leaders to "lean in" and strengthen and modernise the fundamental parts of the UN system.

"Sovereignty, prosperity and peace are never guaranteed—they must be created, nurtured and protected by each generation," Albanese says."We know that the surest way to minimise the potential for conflict is to create the prosperity, opportunity and economic justice on which lasting peace depends."

Albanese to address UN General Assembly soon
We expect Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to step up sometime soon to address the United Nations General Assembly.

It's understood he'll urge nations to come together and cooperate to confront the major challenges facing the world, including climate change, emerging technologies like AI and the breakdown of international rules.
Standby! We'll bring you his speech to the high-level week of the 81st session right here on the federal politics live blog.
Govt wants to see AI hack taskforce report back as soon as possible: Watt
After the announcement of the OpenAI agent Services Australia portal hack yesterday, the federal government set up a taskforce.
Anthony Albanese said yesterday the taskforce would provide an "urgent and immediate review" of the incident.
This morning, Australia's National Cyber Security Coordinator told the ABC the taskforce has already convened.
Environment Minister Murray Watt says he's not aware whether the taskforce has a deadline.

"What this task force is looking at is, what changes to legislation we may need, to prevent these kind of incidents occurring in the future, whether, the circumstances here allow for charges to be laid by the AFP," Watt says."Certainly it's something that we want to see report back as soon as possible."

"What this task force is looking at is, what changes to legislation we may need, to prevent these kind of incidents occurring in the future, whether, the circumstances here allow for charges to be laid by the AFP," Watt says.
"Certainly it's something that we want to see report back as soon as possible."
Watt defends timing of AI portal hack information release by PM
Environment Minister Murray Watt has stepped up for a press conference in Brisbane to discuss renewable energy.
He's announced the federal government has granted the 150th environmental approval for a renewable energy project in Queensland.
But Watt has been asked whether the PM's decision to announce the OpenAI portal hack yesterday was "political".
The minister says it was about the government making sure it had all the information and clarifying what had happened.
"We don't want to be going out half-cocked and providing information that turns out to be incorrect," Watt says.

"We wanted to understand exactly what had happened, what information had been accessed, whether it was a malicious attack or not. And once we had that information available, that was the appropriate time for it to make it public."
Analysis: When rogue AI agent 'scaled a fence', it reinforced Albanese's case for tough guardrails

The revelation that an AI agent went rogue and breached a firewall to get at Medicare statistics has strongly reinforced Anthony Albanese's case for tough guardrails on this transformative technology.
The timing of the disclosure (and the incident itself) is politically fortuitous, although the opposition's suggestion the announcement was delayed for political purposes doesn't hold water.
The government says ministers learned only late last week about the breach. The impact on Albanese's argument would have been the same even if it had been announced a few days ago.
During the United Nations' leaders week in New York, the prime minister has heavily focused on AI, in concert with other like-minded countries, stressing that action is imperative.

Key Event
McKenzie says decision to release OpenAI hack details yesterday was political
Bridget McKenzie says she thinks the prime minister's decision to inform the public of the OpenAI agent hack yesterday was political.
The PM announced yesterday the agent had gained unauthorised access to a Services Australia portal, after speaking with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
The agent accessed the portal on June 18, but the company didn't inform Services Australia until three months later, on September 10, via email.
Katy Gallagher, the minister responsible, didn't find out about the incident until September 17.
The Nationals frontbencher has told ABC Radio National Breakfast it's concerning it took so long for the minister to be informed.
But she says she thinks the decision to release details of the hack when the government did was political.

"I do think that there's undoubtedly been a political decision to delay informing the Australian public, given last week, ministers across the government knew about the breach," McKenzie says."A decision must have been taken somewhere to wait until the prime minister was on the world stage and, for a variety of reasons, made the decision to announce the breach there."

AI Safety Institute's funding level 'appropriate': Charlton
Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton has been quizzed on whether Australia's AI Safety Institute will receive more funding.
The short answer: he thinks the level of funding is "appropriate" and points out the agency was only set up about six months ago.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Charlton says the institute is only one part of the response to artificial intelligence.

"We also have our security agencies, ASD [Australian Signals Directorate], Home Affairs, DST [Defence Science and Technology], all of these agencies work together on AI safety," Charlton says."The AI Safety Institute plays an important role, but it is certainly not the only agency that looks at this issue."
"We also have our security agencies, ASD [Australian Signals Directorate], Home Affairs, DST [Defence Science and Technology], all of these agencies work together on AI safety," Charlton says.
"The AI Safety Institute plays an important role, but it is certainly not the only agency that looks at this issue."
Key Event
Charlton defends disclosure timing of OpenAI portal hack
Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton has defended the federal government over when it informed the public about the OpenAI agent hack.
An OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Services Australia portal on June 18, but the company didn't inform the department until three months later, on September 10, via email.
The PM was informed of the incident on September 19, and raised the matter with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman yesterday.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Charlton says the Australian Signals Directorate had to first understand whether personal data had been breached.
He says OpenAI's reporting of the incident was "completely inadequate" but stopped short of saying whether the government would pursue legal options.

"It was important for us to be able to determine the type of information that was accessed, in particular to be able to inform Australians about whether or not any personal data had been breached," Charlton says."In this case, we have determined that it has not been breached and then the prime minister then spoke to the CEO of OpenAI and announced this to the Australian public."

"It was important for us to be able to determine the type of information that was accessed, in particular to be able to inform Australians about whether or not any personal data had been breached," Charlton says.
"In this case, we have determined that it has not been breached and then the prime minister then spoke to the CEO of OpenAI and announced this to the Australian public."
Govt will look to take legal action against OpenAI over hack: Watt
Murray Watt has flagged the federal government will be looking to press criminal charges against OpenAI over its Medicare data portal hack.
An OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
But the company didn't inform Services Australia of the hack until three months later, on September 10, via an email.
Speaking to Channel Seven, the environment minister says the government would also be open to changing laws if required.
"We have commissioned a taskforce to do an investigation of this event, and if it is possible to press criminal charges, that will happen," Watt says.

"But if we need to update our laws to improve the requirements for notification of these kind of events, then that's what we'll do. And of course, if there's further safeguards that need to be put in place, that's what we'll do as well."One of the things that they'll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian Federal Police under current Australian law."

"But if we need to update our laws to improve the requirements for notification of these kind of events, then that's what we'll do. And of course, if there's further safeguards that need to be put in place, that's what we'll do as well.
"One of the things that they'll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian Federal Police under current Australian law."
Key Event
Taskforce set up to investigate AI agent hack convenes, cyber security coordinator says
Australia's National Cyber Security Coordinator says a taskforce set up to investigate how an OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal has convened.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the AI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
Upon informing the public of the incident, the prime minister announced a taskforce would investigate further.
Michelle McGuinness says the "very rapid taskforce" has already met after being announced yesterday.
The coordinator says it will work to understand gaps, opportunities and challenges, and bring them forward to the government.

"I think the very quick adoption of a taskforce to understand this exact incident is exactly right and we have had already experts across government convene yesterday after the prime minister announced the taskforce," McGuiness says.
"They'll be looking very closely. We will be looking very closely at what we need to do to adjust and adapt. We have working very hard to adopt to the speed of the technology which is very fast."
OpenAI breach strengthens Australia's case for tougher AI safety rules

An unprecedented breach of a government website by a rogue OpenAI agent will sharpen Australia's push to impose stricter safety, transparency and reporting requirements on artificial intelligence companies.

Findings from a "rapid" forensic investigation into the incident will bolster the federal government's existing work to develop national AI standards governing how the technology operates in Australia.

Despite resistance from the Trump administration, Australia will impose "guardrails" on AI, with Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton declaring tech companies should not unleash unsafe models.

"I think what we're observing at the moment is that a number of the AI models … that they have inside their companies are not safe and they have a lot more work to do to make them safe before they release them to the public," he told the ABC.

Albanese to tell UN leaders they need to band together on AI
The prime minister will tell the United Nations General Assembly the world can only confront the breakdown of international rules and the emergence of AI if leaders band together.
Anthony Albanese will cap off his week-long trip to the United States, delivering Australia's national statement to the UN about 9:20am AEST.
Having launched Australia's campaign this week for a two-year term on the UN Security Council, the prime minister is expected to use his speech to make his case.

It's understood he'll urge nations to come together and cooperate to confront the major challenges the world is facing, including climate change, emerging technologies like AI and the breakdown of international rules.
Albanese has previously said the UN needs to modernise and reform if it's to meet these new challenges, just as it has confronted the big problems of the past.
